summary: The chapter opens with an invocation and Maitreya’s questions about creation, dissolution, and the relationship between earthly beings and heavenly bodies. Parāśar introduces Jyotish and describes qualifications for its students. The main account presents Vishnu, divine powers, and the three Gunas as a framework for cosmic manifestation, preservation, and destruction. It links forms of Ahamkar to divinities, sensory organs, and primordial elements, and distinguishes Jivatma and Paramatma components in beings and Grahas.

summary: This chapter presents a theological account linking Vishnu’s incarnations with the nine Grahas. It distinguishes Paramatmāńś from Jivāńś, identifying Ram, Krishn, Narasimh and Varah as wholly possessing the former. It provides nine Graha–incarnation correspondences and describes divine and mortal portions returning to their respective Grahas, which ultimately merge into Vishnu. The closing passage praises knowledge of Jyotish and attaches religious consequences to its rejection; these are textual beliefs rather than computational rules.

Incarnation classification: Ram, Krishn, Narasimh and Varah are wholly Paramatmāńś; the other incarnations among the ten also contain Jivāńś.
cautions: The chapter supplies theological correspondences, not chart-based calculations or predictive conditions.

summary: This chapter introduces the nine Grahas, zodiac divisions, Lagn, and traditional planetary attributes. It sets out benefic and malefic classifications, strength conditions, dignities, planetary relationships, and proportional effects assigned to sign placement. It also describes calculations for solar-derived UpaGrahas, time-based Kaal Velas including Gulik, and Pranapad. Editorial additions supply astronomical approximations and supplementary interpretations. Bodily descriptions, social classifications, longevity assertions, and birth auspiciousness belong to the text’s historical astrological framework, not validated assessment or guidance.
rule_families: Benefic/malefic classification: uses Grah identity, lunar waxing or waning, and Budh’s association with malefics; editorial additions introduce lunar association and aspect exceptions.
Dignity and proportional effects: uses Grah, sign, and degree to identify exaltation, debilitation, Mooltrikon, or own-sign zones; assigns textual benefic proportions by dignity or host relationship.

Natural, temporary, and compound relationships: natural relations use sign lords relative to Mooltrikon and exaltation; temporary friendship uses relative signs 2, 3, 4, 10, 11, and 12; their combination yields five relationship classes.
Solar-derived UpaGrahas: Dhoom is solar longitude plus 133°20′; Vyatipat is 360° minus Dhoom; Parivesh adds 180°; Chap is 360° minus Parivesh; UpaKetu adds 16°40′, with zodiacal wraparound.

Kaal Vela intervals and Gulik longitude: divide local day or night into eight equal parts; assign seven weekday-order rulers starting with the weekday lord by day or fifth weekday lord by night; Gulik uses the ascendant at the start of Śani’s interval.

Pranapad: converts the given time to Vighatis and divides by 15, adding the resulting zodiacal quantity to solar longitude, with an additional 240° for fixed signs or 120° for dual signs; relative placement from Lagn receives historical birth-omen classifications.

summary: The chapter defines Bhava, Hora, and Ghati Lagnas using elapsed time from sunrise and the Sun’s longitude at sunrise. It describes constructing separate house charts while retaining natal planetary positions. It also derives Varnad from natal and Hora Lagna sign counts and outlines sign-based Dasha direction, duration, and subdivisions. Varnad interpretations concerning longevity and relatives are historical textual claims, not reliable predictions. The chapter distinguishes birthplace-dependent natal Lagna from special Lagnas described as common to all places.
rule_families: Bhava Lagna: Divide elapsed time since sunrise by 5 Ghatis (120 minutes); add the resulting sign-and-fraction displacement to the Sun’s sunrise longitude.
Hora Lagna: Divide elapsed time since sunrise by 2½ Ghatis (60 minutes); add the resulting sign-and-fraction displacement to the Sun’s sunrise longitude.
Ghati Lagna: Treat elapsed Ghatis as signs and divide remaining Vighatis by 2 for angular degrees and fractions; add this displacement to the Sun’s sunrise longitude.
Special-Lagna house charts: Retain natal planetary positions and construct separate house charts referenced to each special Lagna.

Varnad derivation: Count natal and Hora Lagna signs forward from Aries for odd signs or backward from Pisces for even signs; add counts when parity agrees, otherwise take their difference, then locate Varnad using the result’s parity.

Varnad Dasha framework: Start from the stronger natal or Hora Lagna; direction follows natal Lagna parity, durations follow sign counts between Lagna and Varnad, and each subperiod is one twelfth of its Dasha.
data_tables: Special-Lagna time rates: Bhava—5 Ghatis/120 minutes per sign; Hora—2½ Ghatis/60 minutes per sign; Ghati—1 Ghati/24 minutes per sign.
Varnad parity map: Odd—forward counting from Aries; even—reverse counting from Pisces; matching parity—addition; differing parity—difference.
Historical Varnad relative-house associations: 7th—spouse; 11th—elder siblings; 3rd—younger siblings; 5th—sons; 4th—mother; 9th—father.

source_heading: The Sixteen Divisions of a Rāśi
summary: The chapter describes sixteen divisions of a zodiacal sign, specifying subdivision sizes, starting signs, planetary rulers, and deity or designation sequences. Allocation rules depend on sign parity or modality, with a separate unequal division scheme for Trimshāńś and a remainder-based calculation for Shashtiāńś. It also names four Varga classification schemes and assigns titles according to counts of favorable divisions. Favorability includes specified sign dignities and an Arudha-based condition, subject to exclusions involving combustion, defeat, weakness, and adverse states.
rule_families: Parity-based allocation: Horā assigns solar/lunar halves by odd or even sign; Saptāńś, Dashāńś, Chaturvimshāńś and Khavedāńś use parity-dependent starting signs.
Relative-sign allocation: Dreshkan uses the first, fifth and ninth signs; Chaturthāńś uses the four Kendras; Dvadashāńś begins from the natal sign.

Modality-based allocation: Navāńś, Shodashāńś, Vimshāńś and Akshavedāńś specify starting signs by movable, fixed or dual sign type; Saptavimshāńś has a less explicit movable-sign starting instruction.
Subdivision designation sequences: Ordered deity or category lists repeat or reverse according to sign parity or modality, as specified for each division.

Trimshāńś and Shashtiāńś calculations: Trimshāńś uses five unequal spans with planetary rulers, reversed for even signs; Shashtiāńś doubles within-sign degrees and uses a remainder modulo twelve plus one to identify its ruling sign.

Favorable-Varga classification: Counts of qualifying divisions determine titles in four schemes; qualification uses dignity and Arudha-related ownership, with exclusions for combustion, defeat, weakness and adverse Avasthas.

summary: The chapter assigns subjects to sixteen divisional charts and presents weighted Vimshopak strength schemes for four sets of Vargas. It describes proportional scoring, Hora-specific effectiveness, and strength relative to exaltation and the Sun. It also names and groups the twelve houses, then supplements house interpretation with corresponding positions counted from planets. These are traditional interpretive claims; several classifications and calculation details remain undefined in the supplied text.
rule_families: Divisional interpretation: select the Varga assigned to a subject; house-lord placement in malefic Shashtiāńś or benefic Shodashāńś modifies the traditional assessment.
Vimshopak scoring: multiply each division's scheme weight by its Varg Vishwa value, divide by 20, and sum; the text supplies broad result bands.

Exaltation-relative strength: full strength at exaltation or own sign, none opposite exaltation, with proportional interpolation between; dual-sign ownership requires an incompletely explained odd/even distinction.
Hora effectiveness: combine planet identity, solar or lunar Hora, sign parity, and beginning/middle/end position; analogous treatment is stated for other divisions.
Sun-relative effectiveness: full effectiveness opposite the Sun and loss of good effects at identical longitude, with proportional interpolation between.
Supplementary house assessment: examine specified houses counted from planetary reference points alongside the natal house and its lord.

summary: This chapter defines sign-based Drishtis through Movable, Fixed, and Common sign categories. Movable and Fixed signs aspect three signs of the opposite category, excluding the adjacent sign; Common signs aspect the other three Common signs. Planets inherit the Drishtis of their occupied signs, and planets occupying receiving signs are also included. The chapter supplies a directional arrangement of the twelve signs for a square or circular diagram, with an editorial addition allowing either format.
rule_families: Sign-based Drishti: given a sign's category and zodiacal adjacency, Movable signs aspect three nonadjacent Fixed signs, Fixed signs aspect three nonadjacent Movable signs, and Common signs aspect the other three Common signs.
Planetary inheritance and reception: a planet inherits its occupied sign's Drishtis; planets occupying receiving signs are also subject to those Drishtis.

summary: This chapter describes subperiod duration and ordering methods for planetary and sign-based Dasha systems. It gives proportional calculations for Antar and Pratyantar Dashas, equal divisions for Charadi Kendradi and Rāśi periods, and sign sequences based on parity and modality. It also discusses Pak and Bhog signs, proportional Kaal Chakr subperiods, and weighted allocation in Pinda, Ańś and Nisarg Dashas. Strength-dependent selections and editorial clarification limit how completely these methods can be implemented from this chapter alone.
rule_families: Planetary proportional subperiods: multiply the parent period duration by the subperiod lord’s Dasha years and divide by the system’s total Dasha years; ordering starts with the parent lord and follows the system’s planetary sequence.
Charadi Kendradi planetary subperiods: divide the main Dasha by nine; start with its lord, then order planets in Kendras, Panapharas and Apoklimas by strength.

Equal Rāśi subdivisions and ordering: divide the parent period by twelve; choose the stronger of the Dasha sign and its seventh as the Antar starting sign, with direction determined by parity and sequences modified by movable, fixed or dual modality.

Pak and Bhog determination: identify the Dasha Asraya sign as Pak; the text describes initial identity with Bhog and a sign-distance rule when the Dasha Prad sign is even, for Char, Sthir and Trikon Dashas.
Kaal Chakr proportional subperiods: multiply the main Dasha span by the required sign’s Dasha span and divide by the total sign Dasha years.

Pinda, Ańś and Nisarg weighted allocation: select eligible Pachak planets by relationship to the Dasha lord, retaining the strongest where multiple planets occupy an eligible position; normalize their fractional weights to allocate the main period.

Rāśi sequence patterns: movable signs use successive signs; fixed signs use every sixth sign; dual signs use Kendra groups from the starting sign, its fifth and its ninth.
Rāśi direction map: odd signs use onward order; even signs use reverse order.

Conditions include house placement from Lagn or Mangal, planetary dignity, Navāńś placement, strength, lordship, conjunctions and aspects. It associates these configurations with prosperity, authority, family affairs, travel and adversity, and modifies Candr’s favorable effects by waxing or waning phase. Medical, death-related and remedial passages are historical textual material, not reliable predictions or practical guidance.

Association and aspect conditions: Match stated conjunctions, relationships or aspects involving benefics, malefics, Mangal and specified house lords.
House-lordship conditions: Identify stated favorable lordships and the historical adverse claims attached to second- or seventh-house lordship.
Ketu Yog Karak condition: Ketu assumes this role through conjunction with a Yog Karak planet, defined here as lord of a Kendr and a Trikon; favorable effects additionally require strength.
Candr phase modifier: Waxing Candr is said to give the favorable effects fully, while waning Candr reduces their impact.

source_heading: Determination of Longevity through the AshtakaVarg
summary: This chapter presents a historical astrological method for assigning a longevity total from the AshtakaVargas of Lagn and all Grahas. Each Rāśi receives a time allocation according to its Rekha count, using a stated mapping from zero through eight Rekhas. The allocations across all the AshtakaVargas are summed and then halved. The passage provides the allocation table and aggregation rule, but does not specify a conversion convention for combining days and years.

data_tables: Rekha count → allotted span: 0 → 2 days; 1 → 1½ days; 2 → 1 day; 3 → ½ day; 4 → 7½ days; 5 → 2 years; 6 → 4 years; 7 → 6 years; 8 → 8 years.

summary: This chapter describes a traditional method for reconstructing unknown birth particulars from a query chart. It uses the query ascendant’s divisional placements to infer a birth-year indicator, solar half-year, season, month, and solar longitude. Approximate age helps distinguish recurring Jupiter cycles, with an additional trinal-sign adjustment when needed. The text then derives a birth-time interval relative to sunrise from solar longitudes and proposes calculating planetary and house positions for the reconstructed time.

Sunrise-relative birth time: convert the difference between inferred birth solar longitude and sunrise solar longitude into Kalas, multiply by sixty, and divide by the stated Sūrya Spast in Kalas; greater inferred longitude indicates after sunrise, lesser indicates before sunrise.
